newsitem.title: UK: Bolivia-Brazil pipeline to create regional gas grid.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia-Brazil pipeline to create regional gas grid.

text.p: Economic and political reforms have brought a 3,000 km gas pipeline between Bolivia and Brazil's industrial heartland to the point of construction after 30 years on the drawing board, an industry conference was told on Wednesday.
Financing negotiations for the $2 billion pipeline have already begun, marking a major step towards the creation of a regional gas grid linking six countries of South America's southern cone.

"I would not be the least bit surprised if in the next ten years we see Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and possibly Peru all in a vast gas transmission system," said Ken Forrest, director of the British government's Offshore Supplies Office.
The rationale for the project has been obvious for decades -- huge energy demand growth combined with heavy pollution in Sao Paolo, and large gas reserves in Bolivia, Argentina and Peru.
But legislative and institutional problems have until now hindered progress, delegates heard.
The project hinges on liberalisation of Brazil's electricity generation market and the privatisation of Bolivia's state oil company YPFB, for which bids close on December 5.

The pipeline alone is expected to cost $2 billion, but its success hangs crucially on new exploration investment in Bolivia, on another $1.5-2 billion funding for Brazilian gas-fired power generators, and on $1 billion investment in gas distribution and industrial conversion over the next 10 years, according to Richard Souchard of British Gas Global, one of many shareholders in the scheme.

He said key to the progress so far were, first, a gas supply agreement between Brazil's Petrobras and Bolivia's YPFB, second, Petrobras's agreement to underwrite $280 million in Bolivian debt finance and, third, a tax exemption treaty between the two countries.

The pipeline would be funded 75 percent by Brazil and 25 percent by Bolivia, using $715 million equity and $1135 million debt finance. Souchard hoped to obtain funding by the middle of next year, which he described as a "rather challenging timetable".
It will have a 30 million cubic metres per day (mcmpd) capacity, although only eight mcmpd is planned for the first year, rising to 16 mcmpd over eight years.

Carlos Morales Landivar, former Bolivian Energy Minister and current Bolivian Ambassador to the United Kingdom, saw Bolivia as a gas transport hub for the region, and envisaged the pipeline carrying Bolivian, Argentinian and Peruvian gas into Sao Paolo.
"The big prize for all of these people is to somehow get its gas into Sao Paolo," said Souchard.
On the Brazilian side, the government has made a commitment to diversifying its energy sources, increasing gas consumption from two to 10 percent of market share within 10 years.
This would steer the country away from very expensive state-funded hydro-electric power, said Diomedes Christodoulou, a director of BVI Technoplan.
He said some of Sao Paolo's electricity costs $8,000 per kiloWatt (kW), compared to $400 per kW for a typical combined cycle gas plant.
